title: Lead by Compass, Not Calendar
author: Cindy Chance
summary: Executive coach and ethicist Cindy Chance argues that leaders can no longer navigate by plans and quarterly dates, because conditions shift faster than results arrive and attention is fragmented. Drawing on Augustine's view of time as memory and attention, and the Greek chronos and kairos, she proposes an outer and an inner response. Outwardly, leaders should orient by values and purpose, trade fixed milestones for a steady rhythm of sensing and adjusting, watch for the right moment, and mark endings and beginnings on purpose so inertia does not pull the organization back. Inwardly, they should create presence by giving one thing full attention, tending memory so it becomes meaning, and seeking resonance over consumption. She ends by asking new leaders what chapter ended when theirs began.
points: Chance says shifting conditions make plans and quarterly goals unreliable, so leaders need markers that hold, namely values and purpose.
A map shows where things are, but a compass gives direction, so strategy becomes knowing the best direction despite limited visibility.
She recommends a steady rhythm of weekly pauses and monthly reviews in place of fixed milestones, plus attention to kairos, the right moment.
Chapters should be closed deliberately with rituals that harvest what was learned, or inertia keeps pulling the organization back.
Inwardly, leaders reclaim attention through full presence in one thing, reflection that builds meaning, and resonance over consumption.
quotes: We must orient ourselves by what doesn’t expire or shift. If plans and quarterly goals must shift before we reach them, it feels like the present is always shrinking.
Strategy in our times is less about predicting the destination and more about knowing which direction is best and continuing on despite changing landmarks and limited visibility.
A steady cadence of sensing, reflecting and adjusting (a weekly pause, a monthly look back, a season of review) gives structure and meaning regardless of what shifts.
When conditions move fast, the work shifts from executing a schedule to recognizing when the moment is right. That’s a different leadership capacity, closer to discernment than planning.
As a CEO, and across the leaders I work with, I have seen what happens when a chapter is never closed: forces of inertia keep pulling the organization back.
The present is the only place we can act. You know this. It is not a mantra. It is true.
We can no longer mark time by where we planned to be. We have to mark it by who we are and where we find ourselves, right now.
